title: Household cost pressure turns geopolitical risk into substitution, reduced mobility, and unequal financial room
source_unit: UK Office for National Statistics, Public opinions and social trends, Great Britain: May 2026, Opinions and Lifestyle Survey
geography: Great Britain; adults ages 16 and over, 6-31 May 2026 OPN collection period

observations.period: 6-31 May 2026; cost-of-living pressure and household responses

denominator.unit: responding adults in the latest OPN period, from 8,770 sampled households

cost_of_living_increased.unit: percent reporting that their cost of living increased compared with one month earlier

cost_of_living_worry.unit: percent very or somewhat worried about rising living costs

food_price_reason.unit: percent of those reporting increased living costs who cited food-shopping prices as a reason

fuel_price_reason.unit: percent of those reporting increased living costs who cited fuel prices as a reason

energy_bill_reason.unit: percent of those reporting increased living costs who cited gas or electricity bills as a reason

responses.value: 61% spent less on non-essentials, 41% spent less on food shopping and essentials, 40% shopped around more, 35% used less household gas or electricity, and 34% cut back on non-essential vehicle journeys

mechanism.value: Price pressure is converted into household substitution, energy restraint, and reduced mobility rather than appearing only as abstract inflation concern

observations.method: ONS weighted Opinions and Lifestyle Survey estimates for adults in Great Britain; multiple-response items are not mutually exclusive and comparison requires confidence intervals.
observations.uncertainty: The period is short and cross-sectional; reported actions may reflect expectations, recall, seasonality, or overlapping shocks and do not establish a causal effect of any single price change.
observations.subgroup: Adults ages 16 and over in Great Britain; age and sex differences are reported for selected financial measures.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some cutbacks may be temporary budgeting choices or normal shopping optimization rather than hardship; reduced energy use can also reflect conservation preferences.

denominator.unit: responding adults in the latest OPN period

unable_to_save.unit: percent reporting they would be unable to save any money in the next 12 months

unable_to_pay_850.unit: percent reporting their household would be unable to pay an unexpected necessary expense of £850

unable_to_pay_850_age_30_49.unit: percent of adults ages 30 to 49 reporting inability to pay the £850 expense

unable_to_pay_850_women.unit: percent of women reporting inability to pay the £850 expense

income_covers_minimum.unit: percent agreeing or strongly agreeing that household income covers minimum living expenses

mechanism.value: A majority can cover minimum expenses while a substantial minority lacks savings or emergency liquidity, revealing different currencies of household security

observations.method: ONS weighted survey estimates with subgroup comparisons; the bulletin provides confidence intervals and directs users to accompanying datasets for statistical testing.
observations.uncertainty: The £850 measure is hypothetical and does not observe actual payment behavior, assets, debt, or informal support; subjective minimum expenses vary across households.
observations.subgroup: Adults ages 16 and over, with comparisons by age and sex; the bulletin notes greater uncertainty for some smaller groups.
observations.counterinterpretation: Inability to pay a specified expense may reflect a preference to use credit or other support rather than no access to resources, while agreement that income covers minimum expenses does not imply discretionary room.

observations.period: 6-31 May 2026; international conflict translated into household exposure

denominator.unit: responding adults in the latest OPN period

international_conflict_worry.unit: percent very or somewhat worried about international conflict

fuel_availability_or_prices.unit: percent selecting fuel availability or prices as a conflict-related worry

energy_supply_or_prices.unit: percent selecting energy supply or prices as a conflict-related worry

safety_of_affected_people.unit: percent selecting safety or well-being of people directly affected as a conflict-related worry

travel_disruption.unit: percent selecting disruption to travel or transport as a conflict-related worry

mechanism.value: Geopolitical conflict is perceived through energy, fuel, mobility, and moral safety channels rather than only through foreign-policy opinion

observations.method: ONS weighted OPN estimates of worries associated with international conflict; respondents could select multiple concerns.
observations.uncertainty: Worry is not realized exposure, price impact, or political action; the survey does not identify which conflicts respondents had in mind or how media information shaped responses.
observations.subgroup: Adults in Great Britain, with age differences: worry was higher among adults ages 50 to 69 and 70 and over than among younger adults.
observations.counterinterpretation: Conflict concern can reflect humanitarian solidarity or general uncertainty without changing household behavior; actual supply effects may be limited even when perceived risk is high.

observations.period: 6-31 May 2026; reported goods availability and food variety

denominator.unit: responding adults in the latest OPN period

all_needed_goods_available.unit: percent reporting that everything they needed had been available in the prior two weeks

essential_food_unavailable.unit: percent unable to buy or access essential food items needed regularly

other_food_unavailable.unit: percent unable to buy or access other food items

spent_more_for_normal_purchase.unit: percent reporting they had to spend more than usual to purchase what they normally buy

less_variety.unit: percent reporting less variety in shops than usual

more_shops.unit: percent reporting they had to go to more shops than usual

mechanism.value: Supply and price friction create time and quality costs even when households ultimately obtain a substitute

observations.method: ONS weighted OPN questions on recent goods availability and food-shopping experiences; multiple-response shortage items are not mutually exclusive.
observations.uncertainty: The bulletin measures self-reported availability over two weeks and does not establish store-level shortages, nutritional substitution, or longer-run food insecurity.
observations.subgroup: Adults ages 16 and over in Great Britain; food and goods questions cover household shopping experiences.
observations.counterinterpretation: Most adults reported all needed items were available, and replacements may preserve consumption while shifting time, quality, or price; reported difficulty does not identify deprivation severity.

related_sources.claim: Prior ONS period for comparison of cost-of-living and social-trend measures.
ONS household-finance dataset accompanying the bulletin.
ONS goods-shortage dataset accompanying the bulletin.

boundary: This record adds a comparative household-exposure route from cost and geopolitical concern through substitution, energy restraint, reduced mobility, emergency liquidity, and goods availability. It is a weighted short-period survey of Great Britain, not a household panel, observed transaction record, causal price or conflict estimate, or proof of persistent deprivation.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official ONS bulletin was reviewed for May 2026 sample and weighting notes, cost-of-living responses, emergency capacity, conflict worries, food availability, and shopping-friction measures.
